---
title: Reproducibility
guide-section: "Reproducible requests"
---

A trialforge study is a pure function of its request: the archetype, `n`, the seed, `studyid`{.gd-no-link},
the controls and the defects. The same request gives byte-identical files on every platform, and
from Python and R alike.

## Seeds

Pass `seed=` to fix a study. With no seed, trialforge draws a fresh one and records it, so any study
can be reproduced later:

```{python}
import trialforge as tf

trial = tf.study("vaccine", n=100)
trial.seed
```

```{python}
again = tf.study("vaccine", n=100, seed=trial.seed)
again.define_xml("sdtm") == trial.define_xml("sdtm") and again.truth == trial.truth
```

Seeds are whole numbers from 0 to `tf.MAX_SEED` (2^53, the largest range of integers that R's
doubles hold exactly, so a seed means the same in both languages):

```{python}
tf.MAX_SEED
```

## Random streams

Every random draw comes from a stream addressed by a path under the root seed: the subject, then the
process (adverse events, labs, dropout), then the analyte or term. Because each independent process
has its own stream, changing one part of a study disturbs only what depends on it. More missed
visits change the visits and the measurements taken at them, but not the subjects, their adverse
events or their medical history:

```{python}
base = tf.study("parallel_continuous", n=300, seed=1)
more_missed = tf.study("parallel_continuous", n=300, seed=1, missed_visit=0.2)
{name: base.sdtm[name].equals(more_missed.sdtm[name]) for name in ("DM", "AE", "MH", "SV", "VS")}
```

`tf.stream_seed()` gives the seed of the stream at a path. Integers in the path are indices and
strings are labels:

```{python}
tf.stream_seed(1, ["subject", 17, "ae"])
```

## Across platforms and languages

trialforge doesn't use the platform's maths library for random values (implementations differ in
the last bit from one system to the next) but a pure-Rust one, and its random draws are defined by
the engine, not by Python or R. Golden test cases pin the XPT bytes of reference studies, and the
test suites of both packages check them.

The R package gives the same data for the same request:

```r
library(trialforge)
trial <- study("vaccine", n = 100, seed = 1)
```

R row numbers count from 1 and Python's from 0; `defects.json` is zero-based in both.

## Across releases

The data for a given request can change between trialforge releases, when a model or a derivation
is improved; the changelog says when it does. To reproduce a study exactly, record the trialforge
version with the seed and controls:

```{python}
tf.__version__, tf.core_version()
```
